Name: Jean-Marie Valheur
Question: Was the Civil Rights Movement "woke"?
Answer: Not one bit. Because people had very real issues back in those days. Very real reasons to fight. Just today I learned about a lady named Rosa Lemberg. She was the daughter of a Namibian woman and a British merchant, adopted at birth by a Finnish couple — she was the first black person in Finland, in fact. Lemberg was born in 1875. In Finland, she experienced no racism. She had friendships, formed relationships. Eventually she got engaged to a Russian doctor. But much to her great sadness, he took his own life just weeks before their planned wedding… heartbroken, Rosa sold all her belongings and moved to America at the turn of the century, trying to start a new life. Once in America, she discovered there was such a thing as racism… but she hated being seen as anything other than Finnish — she was a Finnish person first, her partial black ancestry didn’t come into play. Rosa Lemberg married a Finnish-American man. Was active in the Finnish community. When she died, she even died in a retirement home for Finnish-Americans… Yet when Rosa Lemberg died in 1959, she died in a country where some areas were off-limits to her because of her skin color. Something she had never experienced before in life. She should not have been forced to hide into a cocoon of other immigrants from the “old country” just to feel safe and be herself… but she was. Because the Civil Rights movements was extremely necessary as far as movements go. To call it “woke” is to belittle it.

Name: Jean-Marie Valheur
Question: What are some good examples of kindness?
Answer: During the Holocaust it was customary for the Nazis to kill off the weak, young and sickly first and allow the older, stronger Jews to live and work slave labor. The exact procedures weren’t known to those newly imprisoned… but when Ottla Kafka, sister of famed author Franz Kafka, arrived in Auschwitz, she was selected in a “work group”. A nearby group of orphaned children were set aside to and seperated from the adult prisoners… Ottla, a strong woman, couldn’t stand to see the children crying so she insisted on joining them — the Nazi officer in charge of the selection process allowed her to join the frightened young ones. The children, with Ottla in tow, were brought straight to the gas chambers. She died with them, the very same day. Did she know where she was going, did she have any notion of what was to come? Part of me thinks she did. She wasn’t a stupid woman. There were stories being told, there were whispers. And I doubt a man as clever as Franz Kafka himself would have a sister unaware of the darkness of this world. Volunteering to join a group of orphans sent to their deaths and keeping up their spirits in their final moments on earth, is a great act of kindness. Ottla Kafka’s own daughters were born to her former husband, who was Christian. Hence her children were spared. Still, she chose to spend her last moments alive being a mother to those who had no mother or father.

Name: Jean-Marie Valheur
Question: What is the historical basis of the legend of Vlad the Impaler?
Answer: He was literally a real person. Vlad the Impaler was a ruler of Wallachia from 1448 until his demise in 1477. To his enemies in Hungary, Turkey and the German countries, Vlad was an evil villain. To Romanians, he’s a national hero who stood up to powerful forces and prevailed against all odds. Vlad was, first and foremost, an insanely cruel man. His name “the impaler” refers to his greatest joy in life — to impale people. As in, to stick a sharpened piece of wood into a man (or woman’s) backside and slide it through the entire body so that it sticks out on the neck, shoulder or mouth. It would be done in such a manner to keep the victim alive as long as possible. The wooden pole would then be erected and the victim, wriggling, screaming, crying and begging for death, would be witnessed in his or her agony by passerby’s for their sick pleasure. There was a technique to impaling people, a technique perfected by Vlad — the trick was to make the stake follow the spine and not travel through other parts of the body, therefore missing vital organs. By slowly pushing along the length of the spine, a victim’s agony could be delayed for as long as, in the worst and most pitiful cases, several days. Once, just to intimidate the Turks, Vlad impaled 20,000 men in a forrest. Near every tree, a dead or dying man on a stake, as far as the eye could reach. So his enemy knew what fate awaited him. It is no wonder that legends arose of this man. He signed his letters with “Drakulya”. Or Dracula in English. He wasn’t deliberately trying to sound evil, but changing linguistics didn’t help Vlad — his father had been nicknamed “Dracul” or “the Dragon” in medieval Romanian. But in modern Romanian it means as much as “the Devil”. And to his enemies, he was exactly that.

Question: Can you name some famous individuals who have been criticized for taking their "woke" beliefs too far?
Answer: The best example would be Demi Lovato. In 2021 she got into this whole feud with a small frozen yogurt company in California — because it offered too many diet options and low-fat, sugarfree products. Which, get this, triggered Lovato. She said it was “fatphobic” of the company to offer so many options for people who wanted to lose weight. Aside from this, there’s this whole spiel with Lovato’s gender identity — she switched pronouns more often than a runway model switches outfits during a show. She finally dropped it about two years ago, all-but admitting it was a cry for attention when she shared how it had become ‘confusing and exhausting’ even to herself. Name: Jean-Marie Valheur
Question: Do you think art in itself can be evil? Why or why not?
Answer: Yes, art can be evil. French architect surrealist painter Alphonse Laurencic is the best example of this. During the Spanish Civil War, Laurencic designed holding cells for the Spanish government. He built beds in such a manner that the prisoners would roll off them in the sleep. He then build obstacles on the floor making it painful and impossible to sleep on. Furthermore, Laurencic designed the art on the walls in such a manner that the paintings would enduce a state of further mental anguish and depression into prisoners. Through his art, he tried to make the experience of staying in the rooms as unpleasant as humanly possible. The Nazis showed interest in the wicked invention — Heinrich Himmler himself visited the cells in 1940, trying to draw inspiration from them. In the picture above, we can see Himmler seated in the backrgound. No doubt enjoying the wicked atmosphere “surrealist torture chamber”. Can art be evil? I’d argue Alphonse Laurencic proved that, yes, art can be evil.
